aspectTitle: Headings and labels that are present and topically true but too generic/boilerplate to orient (Information, Section 2, Value, Details)
aspectDescription: The hardest real-world 2.4.6 calls are headings and labels that are not WRONG but are uselessly generic and therefore non-orienting: section headings like 'Information', 'More', 'Details', 'Section 2', 'Content', 'Misc', or field labels like 'Field', 'Input', 'Value', 'Setting 1'. Each one technically relates to the content beneath/within it, so a naive topic-match passes, yet it defeats the Understanding intent that a user can 'find the information they seek more easily' and 'predict what each section contains'. A heading 'Information' over a refund-policy section is true-but-not-descriptive;
scenario: E-commerce 'Orders & Returns' help page whose three sections (refund policy, delivery times, two-year warranty) are all headed 'Information', 'More Information', 'Additional Information' — each heading topically true of the substantive, distinct content beneath it but giving no predictive cue about which section holds what.
mechanism: Heading limb (b49b2e): correctly-nested, non-empty <h2> headings that are topically related but non-descriptive. A screen-reader heading-list / in-page ToC collapses to 'Information / More Information / Additional Information', conveying nothing about refund-vs-delivery-vs-warranty, so the user cannot find or predict section content (fails TT 10.A: heading must describe topic/purpose of its content).

aspectTitle: Repeated or near-identical headings/labels among siblings that fail to differentiate sections (relational/uniqueness facet of G130)
aspectDescription: G130 states descriptive headings identify sections 'in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page', so descriptiveness is partly RELATIONAL: a heading or label can describe its own content yet fail to distinguish it from a sibling, defeating heading-to-heading and skim navigation. Real failures: three accordion panels all headed 'Description'; multiple product cards each headed 'Product'; two form fieldsets both holding inputs labeled 'Name' with no Shipping/Billing qualifier on the field; tabs all labeled 'Details'. Each heading/label is individually p
scenario: E-commerce houseplant listing: a 3-column grid of six product cards where every card's <h3> heading reads the single word 'Product'; the distinguishing species name (Monstera, Snake plant, ZZ plant, etc.) lives in a non-heading span in the card body. The generated heading list reads 'Product, Product, Product, Product, Product, Product'.
mechanism: Heading limb of G130 (relational/uniqueness): each <h3> is individually plausible (each card IS a product) but the six sibling headings are identical, so a screen-reader user jumping H3-to-H3 or opening the headings rotor gets no differentiation between products. The species name is in span.name, which is not part of the heading text and so never appears in the heading list. Confirmed via Chrome accessibility tree: heading list = 'Product' x6.

aspectTitle: Graphical/icon-only labels whose glyph is misleading or context-dependent for the control's real function
aspectDescription: The Understanding text devotes three paragraphs to icon labels: an image can BE a descriptive label, but 'the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts' — a magnifying-glass icon next to a text field reads as 'Search', the same icon on a picture reads as 'zoom/magnify'. 2.4.6's label limb and TT 5.B ('The label or instruction can be graphical or textual') therefore require a human visual judgment: is THIS glyph, in THIS placement, a commonly-understood cue for the control's actual function? Failures are present-but-misleading icons: a floppy-disk icon labeling a 'Send' bu
scenario: Document/PDF viewer toolbar: a magnifying-glass icon button with accessible name "Search" actually opens a print-preview dialog. The loupe glyph and the accessible name agree with each other (loupe=Search) but both misdescribe the control's real function (print preview); the page has no search feature at all.
mechanism: Button exposed as role=button, accessible name "Search" computed from aria-label (inner loupe SVG is aria-hidden). A SR user hears "Search, button" and a sighted user reads the universally-understood loupe, both led to expect text search; activating instead opens a print-preview <dialog>. The graphical label is not a commonly-understood cue for the actual function, failing the 2.4.6 label limb (TT 5.B) though name presence (4.1.2) is met.

scenario: Webmail compose action bar: the primary submit button carries accessible name "Send message" and sends the email, but its only visible label is a floppy-disk SVG — the near-universal "Save"/"Save draft" glyph. A user scanning by icon reads the floppy disk as "save a draft" and may click expecting to save, only to dispatch the message.

The SR-announced name is correct, but the sole visible label for sighted/low-vision/magnifier users is a floppy disk, the commonly-understood cue for save, not send (whose convention is a paper plane/arrow). The graphical label is not a commonly-understood cue for the control's true function, failing the 2.4.6 label limb (TT 5.B); name presence (4.1.2) passes.

scenario: Online-banking dashboard: the only session-end control is a top-bar icon button rendering a gear/cog glyph (universally "Settings") with accessible name literally "gear" (the name names the glyph, not the function); clicking it ends the secure session (log out). Both the glyph (gear=settings) and the literal name ("gear") point away from the real function, with real consequences in a banking context.

scenario: Recipe page action bar with two visually identical heart toggle buttons side by side: one saves the recipe privately to the user's own cookbook, the other posts a public like attributed to the user. scenario: E-commerce product page (PASS control): the same magnifying-glass glyph is used in two places, each correctly. In the header a loupe trails a text field named "Search" and submits a product query; on the product photo the same loupe (with a small +) is named "Zoom image" and opens an enlarged lightbox. This is the canonical context-appropriate reuse described verbatim in the SC 2.4.6 Understanding doc, so the graphical labels are descriptive and the page passes; included to contrast appropriate reuse against the misuse in case-01..05.

aspectTitle: Labels that name the field's topic but omit required data-format / data-requirement cues (format, required, data type)
aspectDescription: 2.4.6's label limb is not satisfied merely by a label that names the field's topic; per TT 5.B and G131 the label must make the field's purpose AND its applicable data requirements clear. A label like 'Date of birth:' on a native date picker is the ACT canonical pass, but real failures are subtler: a free-text field labeled only 'Date' that silently demands MM/DD/YYYY; an 'Amount' field that secretly rejects a currency symbol; a 'Card number' field that only accepts un-spaced digits; a required field whose label gives no required indicator while siblings do. The label is present, grammatically
scenario: UK borough council 'Report a missed bin collection' form: a plain text input (not type=date, so no native picker hints at order) labelled only 'Date' whose JS validator silently accepts only day-first DD-MM-YYYY and rejects 11/06/2026, 2026-11-06, '6 November 2026'. The DD-MM-YYYY format is disclosed for the first time only in the post-submit error.
mechanism: Label names the topic ('Date') correctly and is associated + non-empty, but communicates none of the applicable data requirement (day-first DD-MM-YYYY). The format constraint lives only in the submit-handler regex /^(0[1-9]|[12]\d|3[01])-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])-\d{4}$/ and the after-submit error, which TT 5.B's Note says is insufficient. A screen-reader user hears 'Date, edit text' and cannot know the field rejects reasonable inputs.

scenario: Nonprofit donation form with a legend 'Fields marked (required) must be completed.' Two fields are labelled 'First name (required)' and 'Gift amount (required)'; a third field that is ALSO required (has the required attribute, blocks submit, receives the receipt) is labelled only 'Email' with no '(required)' word, silently breaking the page's own stated convention.
mechanism: The label 'Email' names the topic correctly and the field carries a real required attribute, but the visible label omits the required-status cue that the page taught the user marks mandatory fields and that sibling labels carry. The descriptiveness shortfall is that the label fails to convey the required data requirement TT 5.B enumerates and G131 says a label may carry.

scenario: E-commerce bike-shop checkout. Sibling fields carry their format inline ('Expiry (MM/YY)', 'Security code (3 digits)') but the card-number field is labelled merely 'Card number'. Its validator is /^\d{16}$/ — it accepts only 16 bare digits and rejects the grouped form '4111 1111 1111 1111' that is printed on the card and that nearly everyone types. No mask, no inline cue; the format appears only in the post-submit error.
mechanism: Label states the topic ('Card number') but not the applicable data type/format (exactly 16 digits, no spaces). The constraint lives only in the /^\d{16}$/ submit handler and the error message. The contrast with sibling labels that DO show their format sharpens the shortfall — the field with the strictest, least-obvious constraint is the one missing its cue.

aspectDescription: 2.4.6's label limb is not satisfied merely by a label that names the field's topic; per TT 5.B and G131 the label must make the field's purpose AND its applicable data requirements clear. A label like 'Date of birth:' on a native date picker is the ACT canonical pass, but real failures are subtler: a free-text field labeled only 'Date' that silently demands MM/DD/YYYY; an 'Amount' field that secretly rejects a currency symbol; a 'Card number' field that only accepts un-spaced digits; a required field whose label gives no required indicator while siblings do. The label is present, grammatically
scenario: SaaS workspace signup. The password-creation field is labelled 'Password' with a visible help line that only says 'Choose something memorable' — friendly but misleading. The real complexity rules (at least 12 characters AND at least one symbol) are enforced only by the submit handler and disclosed only in the error after a rejected submit: error-as-format.
mechanism: Neither the label ('Password') nor its associated instruction ('Choose something memorable') communicates the applicable data requirements (>=12 chars, a symbol); the rule lives only in the validator (v.length>=12 && /[^A-Za-z0-9]/.test(v)) and the post-submit error. Presence of a label and an instruction satisfies 3.3.2/4.1.2, but the descriptiveness limb fails because the requirement surfaces only on error — which TT 5.B forbids.

Its validator /^\d+,\d{2}$/ accepts only a comma decimal with exactly two fraction digits and NO currency symbol and NO thousands separator (e.g. '85,00'); the natural German entry '85,00 €' is rejected solely for the euro sign, as are '85.00' and '1.250,00'. aspectTitle: Button/control labels (text) that do not make the control's function clear — generic, ambiguous, or mismatched action verbs
aspectDescription: TT 5.B has a second explicit prong: 'Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function', and G131's whole objective is that 'the label for any interactive component makes the component's purpose clear.' A textual button label can be present and grammatical yet fail to convey the action: a row of 'Submit'/'OK'/'Go' buttons that each do different things; a 'Continue' button that actually deletes a draft; multiple 'Edit' / 'Remove' buttons in a list where the label alone does not say WHAT is edited/removed; a primary button labeled 'Click here'. This is a
scenario: A SaaS analytics dashboard editor raises an unsaved-changes alertdialog whose three action buttons are ALL labeled 'OK'; they respectively save (persist edits), discard (revert), and export (.json), and are even rendered in a different order than the prose lists them. The visible button label alone never says which 'OK' does which.
mechanism: Three sibling controls perform three distinct consequential functions (save/discard/export) yet share the generic, verb-less accessible name 'OK'. The label conveys only 'this is a confirm button', not WHICH function; the disambiguating prose is present but not associated with any button, and DOM order does not match prose order. A screen-reader user tabbing the dialog hears 'OK, OK, OK' and cannot tell save from discard from export — failing TT 5.B's button-function prong (G131: label must make the component's purpose clear).

scenario: A four-step pet-insurance quote wizard showing 'Review' as step 3 (with 'Done' still ahead) has a primary button labeled 'Continue'. aspectTitle: Heading/label descriptiveness that holds in source order but breaks under visual reading order, or for collapsed/dynamic content
aspectDescription: The b49b2e rule's own Assumptions name two hard cases it never instantiates: (a) divergence between flat-tree order and visual reading order via CSS positioning/grid/flex order, and (b) headings for expandable/collapsed (hidden) content. A heading can be descriptive of the content that follows it in the DOM but sit visually above unrelated content (CSS order reorders columns/cards), so a sighted user sees 'Pricing' over the FAQ block; or a heading describes content that is only correct once a panel is expanded, while the collapsed default exposes a different (mismatched) summary. Judging these
scenario: E-commerce product page: a CSS grid-template-areas layout places the DOM-adjacent 'Shipping & returns' <h2> into the top-right grid cell, so it renders visually directly above the unrelated customer-reviews block. The heading is descriptive in flat-tree order but mis-orienting on screen.
mechanism: A heading describes the content following it in the flat tree (shipping text) but CSS grid-area places its rendered cell directly above the customer-reviews panel; a sighted/low-vision/magnifier user perceives the 'Shipping & returns' heading over five-star reviews — the visible heading-to-content relationship is wrong (TT 10.A), while the screen-reader flat-tree order is correct.

Screen-reader flat-tree order keeps each heading glued to its matching content, so this is purely a rendered visual-order failure (TT 10.A).

scenario: Higher-ed course FAQ accordion: each trigger is a real button (aria-expanded/aria-controls) that functions as the section heading, but in the collapsed default every visible trigger reads the generic 'Read article →'. scenario: PASS boundary: an analytics dashboard using the SAME risky techniques as the failing cases — CSS grid-template-areas board + a <details>/<summary> disclosure — but applied correctly. The untested gap is when the visible text and the accessible name DIVERGE in descriptiveness. A field visibly labeled 'First name' but given aria-label='field1' (sighted user fine, screen-reader user stranded); or the reverse, a visibly cryptic 'X' button whose aria-label='Close dialog' is the descriptive one; or a heading visibly reading 'Quarterly Earnings' whose aria-labelledby points at a stray 'Q' so AT announces just 'Q'.
